name: Kashibo-Kakataibo
confidence_why: Zariquiey's 2011 reference grammar, the only source that describes the system, puts primary stress (vowel lengthening) on the first syllable of every two- and three-syllable word and of every non-predicate, with predicates of four or more syllables stressing the head of the last trochaic foot and a separate weight-sensitive high tone on the rightmost prominent syllable, so the initial-stress record is correct as far as it goes but rests on a single first-hand grammar.
catalog_citation: Zariquiey Biondi, Roberto. 2011. A grammar of Kashibo-Kakataibo. PhD thesis, Research Centre for Linguistic Typology, La Trobe University, Bundoora (April 2011). Open download:https://opal.latrobe.edu.au/articles/thesis/A_grammar_of_Kashibo-Kakataibo/21844767(DOI 10.26181/21844767.v1).
catalog_quote: The metrical system is trochaic, that is, feet are left-headed. These trochaic feet are created from left to right (i.e. from the beginning to the end of words). Generally, metrical feet in Kashibo-Kakataibo have to be disyllabic and degenerate feet are only admitted under very specific circumstances (see §4.3.6). In addition, the position of the primary stress (manifested as vowel lengthening) follows a different principle for predicates and non-predicates. Predicates carry the primary stress on the head of the rightmost (i.e. last) foot. Non-predicates carry the primary stress on the head of the leftmost (i.e. first) foot. ... Since tone (but not the vowel lengthening associated with stress) is sensitive to syllable weight ... [Table 21, stress column] phonetic correlate: vowel lengthening / non-sensitive to syllabic weight / metrically assigned / a primary stress on the first metrical head counting from the right to left in predicates, and from left to right in non-predicates / stress-bearing unit: syllable / obligatory / culminative ... [p. 134] Thus, regarding stress, we always find (»σ.σ)σ in trisyllabic words. ... [p. 136] In non-predicates, the primary stress falls on the leftmost metrical head; and in predicates, the rightmost metrical head carries the primary stress. ... [p. 141] There is always a primary stress on the head of the only foot of the prosodic unit to the left. This happens in both predicates and non-predicates.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress (realised as vowel lengthening, not pitch) is metrical and weight-insensitive: disyllabic trochees are built from the left edge and no degenerate feet are formed. Non-predicates (nouns and other words in citation/argument use) carry primary stress on the first syllable, the head of the leftmost foot. Predicates carry primary stress on the head of the rightmost complete foot, i.e. the penult in even-numbered and the antepenult in odd-numbered syllable counts (e.g. (pi.a)(KË.xa) 'ate long ago'). A high tone, treated as a separate feature, goes on the rightmost prominent syllable (the stressed syllable or a closed syllable in even position to its right); a word's final syllable cannot carry it unless lexically marked. Alternative catalog reading: tone language with a stress statement, since the author describes a system combining stress and (non-obligatory) high tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Heads of non-primary feet carry secondary stress, realised as a vowel longer than in non-prominent syllables (§4.3.3, p. 135-136: (»ba.ka)(«ka.ma) 'river=PLU', («pi.a)(»kë.xa)). Trisyllables form one foot only; the third syllable takes no secondary stress and stays short (p. 133).
new_statements.exceptions: A separate high tone (non-obligatory, non-culminative, weight-sensitive, partly lexical) regularly falls elsewhere than the stress: disyllables with a final consonant (overt or underlying) have stress on syllable 1 but high tone on syllable 2 (§4.3.1.2-3, pp. 128-131); some monomorphemic tri-/tetrasyllabic words have a lexical high tone on syllable 2 while stress stays on syllable 1; a few suffixes (e.g. -ín 'proximal') carry lexical high tone without stress (§4.3.9); monosyllables surface with extra-long vowels to satisfy the minimal-word requirement (§4.3.5); Shell (1950, 1987) had analysed the high pitch as stress. Author calls the account preliminary (p. 121).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word: stress is obligatory and culminative per phonological word (definition (150), p. 167: a unit of at least two syllables/one foot and one stress); each word in an NP has its own primary stress; grammatical words of five or more syllables may split into two prosodic units each with a primary stress; adverbial enclitics may carry their own stress. 'Predicate' vs 'non-predicate' is a syntactic-function split, not noun vs verb (fn. 28, p. 124): most words can be predicates and are then prosodically treated as such; nominalised verbs count as non-predicates. Data are instrumentally measured (Praat) elicited words and sentences from two adult male speakers of the Lower Aguaytía dialect.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted description is of the Lower Aguaytía dialect of Kashibo-Kakataibo (Zariquiey 2011, Tables 12-13 and p. 74), the same language-level languoid cash1251 [cbr]; author names the language Kashibo-Kakataibo (2011) / Kakataibo (2018). Older sources call it Cashibo.

new_statements.quote: The assigning of stress and pitch follow different rules depending on whether the word is mono-morphemic or poly-morphemic. In mono-morphemic words, stress and pitch coincide in the same syllable. That is, they occur together as the realization of stress/pitch. The rules for assigning stress and pitch in mono-morphemic words are summarized in (38) below. (38) a. Stress/pitch falls on the second syllable from the left if it has a coda. b. Otherwise, the first syllable from the left attracts stress/pitch. c. Lexical pitch overrules the rules (a) and (b). [p. 40:] In terms of the vowel duration, this phonetic feature tends to occur in the first syllable regardless of where the highest pitch falls.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog records fixed: initial syllable (initial stress, from Zariquiey 2011: trochaic feet built left to right). Valle's rule (38) for the San Alejandro dialect puts stress AND pitch on the second syllable when it is closed (bënsit [wɨn.ˈsí] 'slim': 'when the second syllable is phonologically closed, this becomes the longest one and attracts the highest pitch'), i.e. a weight-sensitive left-edge window rather than fixed initial; for words with an open σ2 (and for duration in poly-morphemic words) it agrees with initial. The difference is partly dialectal and partly analytic: Zariquiey 2011 (Lower Aguaytía; checked held by the project, p. 124ff) keeps stress = vowel lengthening on σ1 even w…
new_statements.rule_in_words: San Alejandro Kakataibo: stress (= vowel duration, intensity) and pitch (high f0) are distinct correlates. In mono-morphemic words they coincide and fall on the second syllable if it is closed (has a coda, e.g. bënsit [wɨn.ˈsí]), otherwise on the first syllable (isi [ˈí.si]); so prominence sits in a two-syllable window at the left edge, weight (coda) deciding between σ1 and σ2. About 3% of mono-morphemic words carry lexically assigned pitch that overrides this (táin 'salt', 'anáka, loans like 'uchíti 'dog', kuríki 'money'); in those the longest vowel stays on σ1 while the pitch may sit elsewhere. In poly-morphemic words duration tends to stay on the first syllable regardless of where the highest pitch falls (abat-ti [ˈaː.wá.ti]), analysed as pitch assignment ordered before stress assignment. Stress/pitch position is contrastive only in a handful of minimal pairs (kúin 'strength' vs kuín 'cloud', táin 'salt' vs taín 'arrow cane'); a few /o/ monosyllables with an underlying coda ('ok 'tapir', xon 'parrot') have a rising-falling pitch. Abstract: 'Tone is distinctive only in a handful of monosyllabic words. Stress is phonetically realized by duration.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: No productive secondary stress/pitch rule is supported: 'If a rule of secondary stress/pitch assignment were in use in Kakataibo, it would predict that the third syllable would receive pitch, as in rëtëpúni. However, it is found that the third syllable shows a short vowel and a low pitch' (p. 42). Secondary high pitches in long words come from bound morphemes with lexical high tone (-pún 'HOD1', -mí 'CAUS', -tánkëxun, =rá(su) 'DIM2', -bësín, -tán 'IMP.GO'; list (44), 'not exhaustive'); such suffixes can head their own phonological word in words of six or more syllables (§2.6).
new_statements.exceptions: (i) ~3% of mono-morphemic words have lexical pitch violating (38a-b): sets (39)-(42) incl. táin, báin (pitch on σ1 though σ2 closed), 'anáka, achúi, 'unpáxo, chuchúbi (pitch on open σ2), padión, xabiónkë, 'ituín (pitch beyond σ2), loans 'uchíti, kuríki, sontáru; (ii) the folktale name kanchanpúxëkërë with stress/pitch on σ3; (iii) poly-morphemic words: duration on σ1 irrespective of pitch; (iv) /o/ monosyllables with underlying coda show rising-falling pitch; (v) stress/pitch minimal pairs (37): kúin/kuín, báin/baín, runtu/runtú, rái/raí-, táin/taín, tana/taná, tui/tuí-.
new_statements.identity_note: Valle Arévalo 2017 describes the San Alejandro (river) dialect of Kakataibo; the catalog's existing statement (Zariquiey 2011) describes the Lower Aguaytía dialect. Both fall under glottocode cash1251.

tone_statements.quote: El caso más claro es el kashibo-kakataibo, analizado como un sistema acentual y tonal en Zariquiey (2011). … La mayoría de las palabras tiene una (o varias) sílabas con tono alto. Este es sensible a la cantidad, ya que es atraído por las sílabas pares cerradas; si no hay una sílaba pesada, el tono alto recae en la última sílaba acentuada (cf. 18c, d y 19a, b). … En casos como (18f), el autor propone que el tono es asignado lexicalmente … En monosílabos se dan contornos tonales ascendentes y descendentes (18a, b).
tone_statements.translation: The clearest case is Kashibo-Kakataibo, analysed as an accentual and tonal system in Zariquiey (2011). … Most words have one (or several) syllables with high tone. This is quantity-sensitive, since it is attracted by even-numbered closed syllables; if there is no heavy syllable, the high tone falls on the last stressed syllable (cf. 18c, d and 19a, b). … In cases like (18f), the author proposes that the tone is assigned lexically … In monosyllables rising and falling tonal contours occur (18a, b).
tone_statements.locator: pp. 149-151, §4 'Lenguas trocaicas', exx. (18)-(19); also Tabla 1 p. 133 and Conclusiones p. 164 'doble sistema métrico acentual/tonal'
tone_statements.summary: After Zariquiey 2011: trochaic stress cued by duration plus a separate weight-sensitive high tone, by default on the last stressed syllable, lexical in some words; contours only on monosyllables.

readall_conflicts: Neither listed work could be read, so no new source-to-source disagreement was found. One point of tension already inside the record: the catalog entry initial stress (initial stress) and the existing statement's 'fixed: initial syllable' summarise only half of Zariquiey 2011's rule. The same grammar (already held by the project, p. 155 = thesis p. 124, and p. 167 = §4.3.6) says: 'Predicates carry the primary stress on the head of the rightmost (i.e. last) foot. Non-predicates carry the primary stress on the head of the leftmost (i.e. first) foot.' — so initial stress holds for nouns and other non-predicates, while verbs (predicates) stress the head of the last trochaic foot; and a separate, weight-sensitive high tone is placed on the rightmost prominent syllable. The catalog reading is therefore correct for non-predicates but the record should note the predicate/non-predicate split and the tone overlay. Valle Arévalo 2017 (San Alejandro dialect) and the catalog's source Zariquiey 2011 (Lower Aguaytía dialect) agree that default word prominence is on the first syllable, that a closed second syllable attracts the high pitch, that stress (duration) and pitch (f0) are separate correlates that can dissociate, and that a small lexical set (incl. loans and certain suffixes such as -pún) carries unpredictable high pitch. They disagree on the duration correlate in mono-morphemic words with a closed second syllable: Zariquiey keeps the lengthened (stressed) vowel on σ1 with only the…

sources.note: From the abstract alone: Kakataibo has word stress and it conditions how much nasal coarticulation vowels next to nasals get, which adds a phonetic effect of stress to the catalog entry (initial stress with a separate high tone, from Zariquiey 2011). The abstract gives no stress position and says nothing about tone, so it neither confirms nor contradicts the entry's rule.

tone.says: Per the Crossref abstract: first phonetic (aerodynamic) description of nasal coarticulation in Kakataibo; coarticulation occurs wherever vowel and nasal are contiguous, and its amount and pattern depend on the directionality of the process, the presence of a syllable boundary, and stress; the authors 'discuss their interaction with prosody'. The abstract names stress, not tone/f0; whether high tone is measured separately was not seen. Prosody-adjacent laboratory phonetics, not a tone descriptio…
